episode_title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji!

stories.topic: Abbé Faria and the whisper that unfroze him
stories.summary: Amit retells a story Jerry Pinto told him on The Seen and the Unseen. José Custódio de Faria was born in 1756 in Candolim, when Goa was a Portuguese colony. His father was a priest and his mother a nun; they joined the church after having him and separated. A child prodigy famous for his sermons, he was invited as a teenager to speak before the Queen of Portugal in Lisbon. On stage, facing the queen, the royalty and his father, he froze. His father leaned forward and hissed in Konkani, 'Kaator re bhaaji': these are all vegetables, cut the vegetables. Faria later left India after getting caught up in a rebellion, took part in the French Revolution, and was jailed in solitary confinement on an island. There he remembered his father's words, built a mental framework and became one of the fathers of hypnotism. Dumas named a character in The Count of Monte Cristo after him.
stories.insight: Big, frightening moments shrink when you treat them as a pile of vegetables to chop. The same mantra got Faria through a royal hall and a prison cell. Ajay adds that Lisbon was then one of the great cities of the world, so the pressure on the boy would have been enormous.
stories.quote: There is a profound reminder in this that ultimately whatever we do in our lives, it boils down to cutting the vegetables, to building a habit, to routine.

stories.summary: A group was split in two. One half had a week to make a single pot and could spend it researching and planning: reading books, taking courses, working out in theory what makes a perfect pot. The other half was told to make as many pots as they liked and just start. The best pots came from the second group.
stories.insight: You get something right by getting it done repeatedly. Iteration beats planning, which is why Amit tells writers to treat the first draft as the block of stone they will later carve.
stories.quote: The best pots came from the second group, which just went out there, which iterated, which got the job done.

stories.summary: When Ali Abdaal reached a million subscribers, he showed a graph of his growth. It took him half a year, 26 weeks of two videos a week, to reach his 50th video and his first thousand subscribers. His advice to new YouTubers is to make two videos a week for two years, about 200 videos, and not look at the metrics until then. Amit tells Ajay to listen carefully because this applies to their show.
stories.insight: Creators overestimate the short term and underestimate the long term. Everyone is bad at the start, so anyone who needs early validation will quit before they ever get good.
stories.quote: If you are driven by validation, then you will not get that validation because you suck and you'll stop doing it and you'll never get good.

stories.topic: Why Everything is Everything took a year to launch
stories.summary: By August 2022 in Udaipur, Amit and Ajay were sure they would do the show and were debating names. Episode 1 arrived more than a year later. Ajay says the delay came from their dreams of quality: a messy, jugaad-style start didn't meet the bar. Amit disagrees. He grants Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe, but says they weren't sharpening anything. He was simply procrastinating. What got it moving was a chance brainstorm with their producer friend Vartika.
stories.insight: It is easy to pass off procrastination as preparation. The hosts still disagree on this, and the disagreement is the lesson: you need both standards and momentum.
stories.quote: You and I took a long time to get to Ep One because we had some dreams of quality and perfectionism in our minds.

stories.topic: India Uncut: 8,000 posts of thinking aloud
stories.summary: Around 2003-04 Amit started the blog India Uncut, which became hugely popular. He posted about five times a day and wrote around 8,000 posts in five active years. He never worried about getting any of them perfect. A lot of that writing would embarrass him now, but he says it was the journey that made him a better writer and thinker.
stories.insight: Writing a lot in public, without fear of being imperfect, is how you build skill. The embarrassing early work is part of the training, not a failure.
stories.quote: There was no anxiety about getting it perfect. It was me thinking aloud.

stories.topic: The athlete who ran in the rain
stories.summary: Amit remembers an interview from the early 2000s with a top sportsperson. It sounded very Dravid-esque but wasn't Dravid, and Amit has failed to track it down. Asked about his greatest talent, the athlete said: he runs every day at five, and on the morning when he has a cold, has already met the year's goals, has a holiday coming up, it is raining and he doesn't feel like it, he still gets up and runs.
stories.insight: Talent is not only an inborn gift. It can simply be the stubbornness to show up when every excuse is available.
stories.quote: I will still get up and go running in the rain. That's talent.

stories.topic: The trap of things coming easily
stories.summary: Amit admits, with some regret, that for much of his life he leaned on his supposed intelligence. Things came easily: an exam others studied 20 hours for, he could prepare for in 20 minutes. He calls this a trap. You never learn to put in effort, so you struggle when the harder task arrives, and the sense of entitlement means you don't work as hard as you should.
stories.insight: Being labelled smart early can quietly stunt you. Effort is what drives improvement, so praise kids for how hard they try, not for how clever they are.
stories.quote: If other people would have to study 20 hours for an exam, I could do it in like 20 minutes, right? And this is a great trap.

stories.topic: A number painted on his forehead
stories.summary: Ajay says India labels children smart or dumb at an early age, often based on mathematics. He was the lucky child who happened to blossom at the right age, and everyone started painting a number on his forehead. He has seen how harshly this sorting treats everyone else. He and Nitin Pai are planning to write 'heretical things' about the IIT JEE exam.
stories.insight: Early labelling hurts both groups. The 'talented' stop running as hard, and everyone else gets written off. Coming from someone who benefited from the label, the criticism carries weight.
stories.quote: I am that lucky child that I just happened to blossom at the right age and suddenly everybody was painting a number on my forehead.

stories.topic: The one habit Ajay is glad he built
stories.summary: Asked by Amit which habit he is glad he built, Ajay says he has organised his whole life around one goal: more hours each day to read. He keeps getting rid of mundane tasks, avoids having to decide about unimportant things and lightens everyday chores, all to make time to read and think.
stories.insight: A focused life is mostly about cutting things out. Fewer decisions and less clutter leave room for what matters.
stories.quote: I just have managed to organize everything in life around one main purpose, which is to get more hours per day to read.

stories.topic: The notes behind the Ukraine episode
stories.summary: During his Roam Research demo, Amit opens the page for his Seen and the Unseen episode with Ajay on Russia and Ukraine. Ajay had prepared it chapter by chapter, with detailed notes, links and a list of sources at the end, 'like a good academic'.
stories.insight: Deep expertise isn't crammed in the week before. It comes from years of following your curiosity down rabbit holes and organising what you find.
stories.quote: It's not as if you decided a couple of days before the episode, let's talk about Ukraine, let me read up something. Instead, it was a lifetime's habit of reading.

stories.summary: Amit's friend Gautam John once had a rule that he looked at his smartphone, for anything other than calls, only between five and six in the evening. Messages sent at other times would simply wait. He also uses only Signal, not WhatsApp.
stories.insight: You can choose how your attention is divided. Choppy scrolling makes for a choppy mind, so a hard boundary is a practical defence.
stories.quote: So people decide how they're going to apportion their time.

stories.summary: Ajay attended a talk where Rahul Dravid said he never thought about Sachin Tendulkar and only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid he could be. Ajay uses it while arguing that a life built around showing off markers to others is a poor operating system.
stories.insight: Measuring yourself against others drains energy. A purpose aimed at becoming your own best self lasts longer.
stories.quote: I did not think about Sachin Tendulkar, I only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid that I can be.

stories.summary: Amit sometimes asks friends which Seen and the Unseen guest is most likely to win a Nobel Prize. The standard answer is Karthik Muralidharan, who is clearly on that track. Amit's own rule is to name the most brilliant person he knows, which is Ajay. When he told Ajay this, Ajay said it wouldn't happen because he isn't on that track. Amit sadly agrees: Ajay has defined his purpose differently and is playing a different game.
stories.insight: Prizes reward people playing a particular game. Someone driven by curiosity rather than credentials may be brilliant and still choose not to play it.
stories.quote: It's not gonna happen because you're not playing that game. That's a different game.

stories.summary: Donald Knuth spent his life polishing TeX, a professional typesetting system used to set many great books. Now old, he says TeX is finished: it needs no new features and has no recorded bugs. The code is open, and he asks only that anyone who builds on it after he's gone call it something else, because 'this is my Taj Mahal'. When someone does find a bug, Knuth sends them a cheque, and people frame it and hang it on the wall.
stories.insight: Most software is 'rubbish layered on rubbish', always being torn up and rebuilt. Knuth shows that a piece of software can actually be finished.
stories.quote: He says, This is my Taj Mahal, I built this. And I believe it is complete.

recommendations.creator: James Clear
recommendations.context: Amit's main recommendation of the episode. He also quotes it in the 'habits are everything' section.
recommendations.reason: The best book on productivity he has read. Much of what he knows about productivity comes from it, and it led him to many other books. If you read only one book on the subject, start here.

recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: Amit's end-of-episode recommendation, following his use of Abdaal's growth graph and creator advice.
recommendations.reason: Useful for figuring out tools, mental models and frameworks. Abdaal started small and grew big, so he has lived his own productivity advice.

recommendations.creator: Thomas Frank
recommendations.context: Recommended together with Ali Abdaal as the channels Amit followed while trying to understand productivity.
recommendations.reason: Another creator who started small and built himself up by practising what he teaches. Good for working out which tools and ways of thinking suit you.

recommendations.item: My Top 10 Tips for Aspiring YouTubers
recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: Amit calls this 'another video by Ali Abdaal which I love'.
recommendations.reason: Source of the advice to make two videos a week for two years without looking at the metrics. It's the antidote to quitting while you're still bad.

recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: The video with the growth graph Amit shows on screen.
recommendations.reason: It shows that 50 videos and half a year of work produced only about 1,000 subscribers. Concrete proof that growth takes a long time to compound.

recommendations.item: The Parable of the Pottery Class
recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for the pottery experiment Amit describes.
recommendations.reason: A short telling of the experiment where the group that made many pots beat the group that planned one perfect pot.

recommendations.item: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
recommendations.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
recommendations.context: The study behind Amit's 'don't be it, just do it' section.
recommendations.reason: Children praised for being intelligent did worse later and sometimes cheated. Children praised for effort kept improving. Useful for parents and for how you talk to yourself.

recommendations.item: How to Enhance Performance & Learning by Applying a Growth Mindset
recommendations.creator: Huberman Lab Podcast
recommendations.context: How Amit came across the Mueller and Dweck study.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great episode of a podcast that is excellent on the whole. An accessible way into the growth-mindset research.

recommendations.context: Amit demos it live, showing his notes for the Ghazala Wahab episode, the Ukraine episode and the previous Everything is Everything episode.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a game changer. Nested entries and two-way links let him find anything without scrolling through 40-page Word files, and help him think in a more structured way. It is based on the Zettelkasten system.

recommendations.context: Mentioned while comparing note-taking and productivity tools.
recommendations.reason: He thinks it's a great productivity tool, though he hasn't really started using it. Roam suited his wish for a loosely organised knowledge system better.

recommendations.context: Amit mentions that Nitin Pai and colleagues at Takshashila use it well and that it's free. Ajay adds his reasons.
recommendations.reason: It is easy to run locally on Linux and stores notes as plain Markdown files, so the whole Unix toolchain can work on them.

recommendations.creator: Tiago Forte
recommendations.context: Raised after Roam, as the bigger idea behind note-taking tools.
recommendations.reason: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool for retaining knowledge. Forte's idea of using technology as a second brain addresses the fact that we lose most of what we take in.

recommendations.creator: Richard Stallman and James Gosling
recommendations.context: Ajay's answer to Amit's wish for a do-everything Swiss army knife, and again in his Unix recommendation.
recommendations.reason: A mature editor with a fully programmable interface. A few hundred lines of Lisp let you build your own productivity world on top of it, and thousands of existing extensions mean you don't start from scratch.

recommendations.context: Ajay's alternative to Roam Research.
recommendations.reason: It does much of what Amit demoed in Roam and is very powerful. Its one gap is a shared, networked file for collaborators, so it is best for solo work.

recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation of the episode, making up for skipping one the week before.
recommendations.reason: After 40 years around computers, he considers it the most productive and powerful environment there is. Small tools are strung together to do any task. Unix runs under Macs, Chromebooks, Android, Kindle and Linux, and he sees it as a philosophy as much as software.

recommendations.creator: Donald Knuth
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of how mature the Unix toolchain is.
recommendations.reason: A professional typesetting system used for many great books. Its author considers it finished and it has no recorded bugs, a rare level of craftsmanship in software.

recommendations.context: Listed while Amit describes his workflow and his fantasy of building one app that combines them all.
recommendations.reason: The specialised tool for writing screenplays. Useful, though he sees such apps as pocket calculators that could become far more.

recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside Final Draft.
recommendations.reason: The tool for writing books, another of the single-purpose apps Amit has used.

recommendations.creator: David Allen
recommendations.context: Ajay brings up GTD ('do, defer, delegate') as part of the productivity-techniques world. Amit recalls it is a David Allen book.
recommendations.reason: Named as the classic of the productivity-tools-and-procedures tradition, which Ajay questions as too managerial.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The episode where Jerry Pinto told Amit the Abbé Faria story.
recommendations.reason: An eight-and-a-half-hour oral history that Amit calls fantastic. Its Faria story inspired him and many listeners.

recommendations.item: Abbé Faria: The Hypnotic Story of A Goan Son
recommendations.creator: Carol Lobo
recommendations.context: Show-notes link for readers who want more on Abbé Faria.
recommendations.reason: Background on the Goan prodigy who became one of the fathers of hypnotism.

recommendations.creator: Alexandre Dumas
recommendations.context: Mentioned at the end of the Faria story.
recommendations.reason: It has a character named after Abbé Faria, which links the episode's mantra to classic literature.

recommendations.item: The BJP Before Modi (Episode 202, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's first episode with Vinay Sitapati, which included an hour-long discussion on writing.
recommendations.reason: Source of Sitapati's line 'Never let perfection be the enemy of production'.

recommendations.creator: Ghazala Wahab
recommendations.context: The book whose chapter-by-chapter notes Amit uses to demo Roam.
recommendations.reason: He points to her sentence about her grandfather shelling pine nuts all day to reward the children as a model of showing rather than telling.

recommendations.item: Being Muslim in India (Episode 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The episode with Ghazala Wahab that the Roam notes were prepared for.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great episode. It shows what his note-taking process produces.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Shown in the Roam demo with Ajay's chapter-wise notes and sources.
recommendations.reason: Built on a lifetime of reading rather than last-minute research, which you can hear in the episode.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit shows their joint Roam notes for the previous episode: the Angus Maddison chart, pre-91 India, a Bhagwati quote, a Friedman memorandum.
recommendations.reason: Shows how the hosts prepare together and how they changed the structure on the fly.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay links the CGM (continuous glucose monitor) discussion to habit formation.
recommendations.reason: A worked example of focusing hard on one habit for a few months and then letting it run on autopilot.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 piece on education, which he recalls while discussing how Indian children are labelled.
recommendations.reason: It makes the supermarket point: a thousand brands of shampoo to choose from, but no such choice in education because markets aren't allowed to function there.

recommendations.item: Doing better than a competitive exam
recommendations.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link tied to Ajay's remark that he and Nitin Pai plan to write 'heretical things' about the IIT JEE.
recommendations.reason: Questions India's habit of sorting and ranking students through one exam.

recommendations.creator: Walt Whitman
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Whitman before contradicting his own first piece of advice.
recommendations.reason: The source of 'we contain multitudes', Amit's excuse for offering advice that contradicts itself.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Show-notes link for the line Amit attributes to either Hitchens or Dawkins, that believers are atheists about every religion but their own.
recommendations.reason: It sets up Amit's argument that we are all stupid about almost everything.

recommendations.item: Episodes of The Seen and the Unseen with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Karthik comes up as the standard answer to 'which guest will win a Nobel'.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls him a brilliant economist doing amazing work who is clearly on that track.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The writing course Amit keeps drawing on for examples: first drafts, 200 words a day, verbs over adjectives.
recommendations.reason: Many of the episode's habit and iteration ideas come from what he teaches his writing students.

core_ideas.concept: Kaator Re Bhaaji: cut the vegetables
core_ideas.explanation: The episode's mantra. However grand or frightening a task is, it comes down to the next concrete piece of work, done routinely. Stop staring at the audience and start chopping.
core_ideas.quote: All these are vegetables. Cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables.

core_ideas.concept: Getting it done vs getting it right
core_ideas.explanation: Every project involves a trade-off between finishing and perfecting. Amit leans towards finishing. The first draft is a brain-dump, like the block of stone Rodin started with before The Thinker. Getting it right comes from getting it done again and again, or as Vinay Sitapati puts it, never let perfection be the enemy of production.
core_ideas.quote: You get something right by getting it done again and again and again.

core_ideas.concept: You suck at the start, so ignore validation
core_ideas.explanation: Everyone begins badly. If you need early feedback to keep going, you will quit before you improve. Creators overestimate what happens in the short term and underestimate the long term, so keep going without checking the numbers.
core_ideas.quote: Whenever you start something, you suck at the start. This is a fact of life.

core_ideas.concept: Your uniqueness is your edge
core_ideas.explanation: Chasing gaps in the market, trends or the algorithm erases what makes you different. Do what you love and keep repeating it.
core_ideas.quote: The only thing that separates me from the 8 billion people on this planet is me.

core_ideas.concept: Iteration needs a sense of quality
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's counterpoint. Repetition only helps if you feel which way is uphill. Otherwise you can stay bad forever. He calls the celebration of 'jugaad' a fancy name for accepting shoddy work. Push standards ('no, this ain't good enough'), but don't let perfectionism paralyse you.
core_ideas.quote: It is possible to just keep doing the same thing over and over and being bad at it every single time.

core_ideas.concept: Don't do it, just be it
core_ideas.explanation: A schedule-only habit ('read 7-8pm daily') breaks by day three and then damages your self-image ('I'm not a reader'). Instead, decide who the best version of you is ('when I'm bored, I pick up a book, not the phone'). Once you own that identity, the habits follow, and one missed day means nothing.
core_ideas.quote: Where your self-image drives your habits and not the other way around.

core_ideas.concept: Verbs matter, adjectives don't
core_ideas.explanation: Praising traits ('you're so intelligent') creates entitlement and fragility, and in the Mueller-Dweck study such children did worse and sometimes cheated. Praising actions ('you tried, you persisted') keeps people improving. Talk to children about effort, persistence and habits, not cleverness or looks.
core_ideas.quote: Those that you grade on their effort, that is where you use verbs, you tried, you worked, you persisted, you know, those are the ones that continue doing well.

core_ideas.concept: Show, don't tell
core_ideas.explanation: In writing, a vague adjective like 'a loving grandfather' says little. A concrete action brings the person to life. Amit's example from Ghazala Wahab's book is a grandfather who spends the day shelling pine nuts for his grandchildren.
core_ideas.quote: Never tell a reader something, show it to them. So instead of adjectives, use verbs.

core_ideas.concept: Habits are the whole game
core_ideas.explanation: Put a hundred writers in a room. Their goals won't tell you who is good, but their processes and habits will. Habits compound like interest. Set targets small enough to survive a busy day, like 200 words a day rather than 1,000, because a missed big target starts a 'mujhse nahi hoga' (I can't do this) spiral. A gym membership doesn't build muscle; going does.
core_ideas.quote: You ask them what are their processes, what are their habits and you will know who's gonna make it and who's not gonna make it and you will never be wrong.

core_ideas.concept: One habit at a time, two to three months each
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's method, drawn from his experience with a glucose monitor. Building a habit takes about two to three months of focused monitoring before it runs on autopilot. You can't take on six at once. After that, keep half an eye on it to make sure it hasn't faded, then move to the next.
core_ideas.quote: You have to fight one thing at a time and it is solvable.

core_ideas.concept: No one is watching you
core_ideas.explanation: The deepest anxiety is what others think. Amit only realised in middle age that people are absorbed in their own lives. Social media makes it worse by setting your real self against everyone else's projected self. Drop the comparison and work towards your own best version.
core_ideas.quote: No one is thinking of you, boss. Everyone's got their heads up their own ass.

core_ideas.concept: We are all stupid
core_ideas.explanation: Borrowing the argument that believers are atheists about every religion but their own, Amit notes that each of us knows only a handful of things well. That calls for humility about ourselves and for not judging others by the narrow skills we happen to value. As he puts it, you cannot test fish on climbing trees.
core_ideas.quote: In the vast majority of things, we are stupid.

core_ideas.concept: People blossom at different rates
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says age-sorted classrooms, where every child gets the same curriculum and exams at the same age, are an industrial-revolution idea. Educators know people develop in different areas at different speeds. The aim should be to make the most of each person rather than attach a label and treat it as destiny.
core_ideas.quote: Humans are unruly, unpredictable creatures and we all blossom in different dimensions at different rates.

core_ideas.concept: Curiosity and endurance, not talent
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls 'talent' one of the most harmful words. The real superpowers are curiosity and endurance, fuelled by purpose. Practical goals like a job, a paper or money are weak fuel because once you reach them you are left asking what next. Since the Greeks, we have known that meaning comes from being part of something bigger than yourself, and simple goals use only about ten percent of a person.
core_ideas.quote: The problem with practical goals is that you'll actually achieve them.

core_ideas.concept: The Louis Vuitton bag of credentials
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's name for a life organised around status markers: the famous university, the top journal, the festival book talk, the Paris trip to show off. He calls this a poor operating system because it doesn't engage the mind. In research, he sees 'journal orientation', channelling curiosity into getting published, as toxic because it switches curiosity off. His own path has been dropping these distractions to stay connected to the core.
core_ideas.quote: It's a poor operating system, most importantly, because it actually does not harness the mind.

core_ideas.concept: Thirty years of the same year
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that years alone don't build experience. Writing an eleventh paper like the first ten, or living the same life repeatedly, isn't growth. What changes a year is curiosity, endurance and willingness to challenge the status quo, which is why people who prefer to keep things as they are are at a disadvantage.
core_ideas.quote: You could be doing thirty years of the same thing over and over, and you've actually not been on a life journey of growing and becoming a bigger and better and more interesting person.

core_ideas.concept: The form of your tools shapes your thinking
core_ideas.explanation: A day of reading a physical book sets one rhythm of mind; a day of scrolling and swiping sets a choppier one, with shorter attention. Roam's nested, linked structure made Amit think in a more structured way. How you take in and organise information is not neutral.
core_ideas.quote: The form of our input and output matters.

core_ideas.concept: A second brain
core_ideas.explanation: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool and poor at holding knowledge. Taking Tiago Forte's idea, Amit argues for using technology to store and organise what you learn, because otherwise most of it slips away. Whether you use Roam, Obsidian or Org Mode matters less than having the habit.
core_ideas.quote: All day we are taking in learnings that we do not retain.

core_ideas.concept: Old, mature tools are often the best
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay rejects the fashion for the newest thing. Tools that have kept passionate users for decades, like Emacs and TeX, built by great thinkers and polished over years, are usually higher quality than most current software.
core_ideas.quote: Most of the world of software is just some rubbish layered on rubbish.

core_ideas.concept: The Unix philosophy
core_ideas.explanation: Many small tools, each easy to chain together, combined to do any task. Ajay sees it as a way of thinking about computers and the world, not just a system. In his telling the same set of ideas led to TCP/IP, the internet and the web, which is why he names Ken Thompson, whose values and taste he credits for it, the greatest man of the last fifty years.
core_ideas.quote: The philosophy is there are many tools and we assemble the tools to perform a task.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens the episode: 'we are at the brink of a great moment in merchandising where the slogan just do it is going to be overpowered by the slogan Kaator Re Bhaaji.' The hosts are wearing Kaator Re Bhaaji t-shirts made by Amit's friend Narendra Shenoy.
Amit on Faria's parents being a priest and a nun: 'don't worry, no hanky panky', since they joined the church after having him.

Amit's dramatic scene-setting in Lisbon: 'an August gathering, though I don't know if it was August', with royalty 'in their breeches and their gowns, with magnificent smiles and frowns', plus a stern 'Don't interrupt the story' to Ajay.
Ajay dates Faria's birth in 1756 as 'before the Battle of Plassey', and Amit replies, 'There you go.'
In the pottery experiment, the planning group gets to take online courses in 'the art of clear pottery', a nod to Amit's writing course, The Art of Clear Writing.

Amit describing a dying reading habit: 'somebody is wrong on the internet, and obviously I have to correct them', after which you decide you're 'a Netflix kind of person, or if I'm adequately gregarious... a Netflix and chill kind of person.'
Amit on owning your identity as a reader: at friends' houses 'the first thing I will check out is their bookshelves. Only then will I say hello to them. I don't do this, by the way.'
Amit on no one watching you: 'No one is taking screenshots and waiting to put it on Twitter to shame you, or actually in my case, they are.'
After Amit's first slogan, Ajay says: 'Very well, Amit. Now contradict yourself.' Amit replies, 'I will contradict myself for we contain multitudes, as the great Walt Whitman once said.'
Abraham Lincoln's line, quoted by Amit, about spending five of six hours sharpening the axe before chopping the tree. Amit then admits the hosts' year-long delay was procrastination, not sharpening.
Rodin and The Thinker: he didn't conjure it from thin air but 'edited the block of stone', which is Amit's picture of a first draft.
Ajay: 'the problem with practical goals is that you'll actually achieve them.' Amit: 'It's like the dog that chases a car and finally catches it and whatcha gonna do then.'
A line Amit attributes to either Christopher Hitchens or Richard Dawkins: believers are atheists about the thousands of other religions, which he turns into 'we are all stupid'.
Ajay mentions GTD and Amit replies, 'You're scaring the shit out of me. What is GTD?'
Ajay dislikes the word productivity because 'it's too much of a managerial thing. It's too much Taylorism for me.'

After Ajay criticises academics chasing 'pubs', Amit says: 'it is not only academics who want pubs. I was once in Europe, it was a hot sunny day, beer peena tha, main pub dhoondh raha tha' (I wanted a beer, I was looking for a pub).
Amit's fantasy of building one app to replace Roam, Notion, Final Draft and Scrivener: 'maybe I can do it one day and I'll get GPT-4 or GPT-5 to code it for me.'
Donald Knuth calls TeX 'my Taj Mahal' and sends cheques to anyone who finds a bug. The finders frame them instead of cashing them.
Asked who was the greatest man of the last fifty years, Ajay picked Ken Thompson, crediting his values and aesthetic sense for the Unix lineage that led to the internet and the web.
Amit after Ajay's Unix tribute: 'What does a Marathi programmer say to another Marathi programmer when he finds a flaw in a computer program? Bug, bug. So anyway, bug is Marathi for see.'
Amit teasing Ajay for skipping last week's recommendation: 'You weren't prepared, which is a great flaw in your productivity processes, after all these things that you say.'
Amit calls the YouTube audience 'gentle readers', and Ajay approves: 'Good old-fashioned 19th century speak.'
Roam Research is based on Zettelkasten, which Amit describes as a German note-taking system.
